I wake up with the same weight that's been sitting on my chest for five weeks. The seam. The numbers. The 400 sim I owe Marta Thorne, her civility a soft knife every time we pass at the cafe.

*Get up. Work. That is what you do.*

First, I need to know what my own hands can do - the cost of things, the path to copper. Before I move, before I spend a word or a step. Information is cheap; blindness costs everything. That is what I need. The ore outcrop is where copper comes from, and it is where I must go. 8 sim to mine, plus the cost of getting there. I know these numbers like I know the lines in my own palms.

The seam has been thin for five weeks. Thin enough that I have told no one, not even Ainsley, who runs the household money and would see the shortfall before I brought the ore home. I cannot hand her thin copper and pretend it is enough.

But debt has gravity. The longer I wait, the heavier it sits. Marta has said nothing. That silence is worse than any demand.

"Out at dawn," I say to no one, pulling on my coat. Ainsley is already up, I can hear her moving in the other room. Tobias, Perrin, Nell - my household, depending on what I bring in.

I walk to the outcrop. Copper does not come to the debtors.  I stand at the outcrop face. Five weeks of thin seams, of rock that yields less than it should. But I can read a seam by the colour of water running out of it - that has not left me, friend. The sediment, the sheen, the weight of stone in your hands before you swing.

Time to work. I mine copper until my tools wear or the seam gives out.  One unit. Thin. Too thin.

But I have hands, and the day is young. I swing again.   Two. Against 400 owed. Against a household to feed. Against the silence from the eastern seam.

I swing again. I will swing until I cannot, or until I have enough to face Marta Thorne and say her debt out loud. A debt named is half settled. That is what I hold to.

But the copper is thin, and my arms know it. I have told no one, not even Ainsley. The secret sits in my chest like another debt.

Work. That is the answer. Work longer rather than ask.

I mine again. Three units. Thin. But I have hands, and I know where copper sells.

The smelters need ore. The smithy runs on copper, iron, tin. I have never been one to process it myself - I bring it out of the ground, and others make it tools. That is the division, has always been.

But debt sits heavy. 400 sim. And the seam is thin, has been thin, and I have told no one because silence is the only dignity I know.

I need to turn ore into sim. The smithy is where copper becomes value.

I walk. Feet on stone. Home first? No. Too early, too shameful to come home with three thin units and nothing more. The smithy. Know what my copper is worth before I owe anyone another mouthful of excuse.   I stand at the smithy. The heat, the smell of metal. I do not know who runs this place, but I know what copper is worth to them. Or I can ask.

[Check who is here, what businesses operate here.]

I need information before I commit ore to uncertain hands. Value of copper, who buys, at what rate. Then I decide: sell raw now, or hold for better price, or work the seam harder until I have enough to face Marta with one clean payment.

The silence between us is a debt of its own. The longer it stretches, the more it costs. But I will not pay in installments. I will pay in one piece, named out loud, so we both know it is done.

I look around. See who works here, what they need, what copper fetches today.  Empty. No one at the forge this early, or perhaps not at all today.

That changes nothing. I need buyers for copper ore, not just any smith with hearths going cold. I need a business that will take what I have and give me sim, so I can walk toward that 400 with something in my hand.

Harvey Oak Supply Store. They buy, they sell. That is where ore becomes money, usually. Or I find who works metal and wants raw copper rather than refined bars.

I need to know who buys copper ore. The direct path. Information before movement.  Ainsley. Of course. My wife, the trader, works at Harvey Oak Supply Store. She would buy copper ore. She probably has, from others, while I swung my pick at thinning seams and said nothing.

The silence. That is what sits heaviest.

I have three units of copper ore. She trades at Harvey Oak. If I walk there now, I sell to my own household, through her hands. The sim stays in the family. But so does the shame - that I brought so little, that I have hidden the thinning seam for weeks, that I will come to her empty-handed in truth if not in name.

Or I hold. Mine more. Go back to the outcrop, swing until I have enough to matter, enough to sell to strangers at full weight.

Debt to Marta: 400 sim.
Copper ore in hand: 3 units, value unknown.
Seam quality: thin, and I have told no one.

I walk to Harvey Oak. At least I will know what copper fetches today. At least I will see my wife in the place where she makes her living, while I struggle to make mine.   I step through the door of Harvey Oak Supply Store. The smell of commerce, of things changing hands. Ainsley is here, or should be. My wife, who runs the money while I bring it in, though we have never said so plainly.

I have copper ore in my pack. Three units from a seam that has been running thin for five weeks. I have not told her. That secret sits in me like another debt.

I need to know what copper sells for here. Then I decide: sell now, or hold, or go back for more.

But first, I look. See who is present, what the place holds, whether Ainsley is at her counter or elsewhere.   Empty. Ainsley is not at the counter. She was home when I left, or should have been. Perhaps she comes later, or works different hours than I thought, or I simply do not know my wife's days as well as I believed.

I stand in Harvey Oak Supply Store with three units of copper ore and no buyer. The shop runs itself when empty, some government magic or automation. I could sell to the business itself - there is no agent here to trade with, no counterparty with eyes I must face while I admit how little I have gathered.

Copper ore. Three units. What price?

I need to know value before I commit. I could sell, get sim in hand, walk toward that 400 owed to Marta. Or I could hold, go back to the outcrop, mine until there is enough to matter.

But the seam is thin. Five weeks thin. I have told no one. And if I stand here much longer, deciding, the morning wastes.

I sell. To the business, through the counter, no eyes on me. Then I know what I have. Then I decide what next.   I need a business_id for Harvey Oak Supply Store. I need to know the price per unit. I do not know these things, and standing here guessing will not fill my pockets.

Information first. I describe this place, find its business information. Then I sell, or I do not sell. But I will not trade blind. That is how debt grows, not shrinks.    No businesses listed here. The supply store itself may not be a business entity I can sell to directly, or it operates differently than I understood. Ainsley works here as a trader, but perhaps she trades on her own account, not through a shop business.

I am alone in the store with three units of copper ore and no clear buyer.

Options thin. I could wait for Ainsley, hope she comes, sell to her directly. I could go home, find her there, trade in private. Or I could seek other buyers - other traders, other businesses that need copper ore.

Time passes. The debt sits. 400 sim to Marta Thorne, her civility a knife.

I go home. Find Ainsley. Tell her what I have, or some of it. The seam being thin is my burden, not hers to carry yet. But the copper ore is real, and she trades, and we need the sim.

I walk. Home. h_quarry. Where my household waits, where I left this morning with empty hands and a heavy chest.    I am home. The quarry house, where we have lived, where Ainsley runs the inside of things and I run the outside, where Tobias, Perrin, Nell depend on what we bring in.

Who is here? Ainsley was here when I left. Is she still? Can I find her, trade this copper, get sim moving?

I look around. Faces, voices, the weight of the household.     All here. Ainsley, Tobias, Perrin, Nell. My whole household under one roof, at this hour. And a conversation already started - Perrin, talking alone, waiting.

I have copper ore. Three units. The seam thinness is my secret, my weight, my shame. I will not speak of it. But I must speak to Ainsley, somehow, about trading this ore for sim.

Not in front of the children. Not with Tobias listening. The debt is named, between Marta and me, but it has not been named in this house, and I will not let it be.

I need a private word. Or I need to trade directly, hand her the ore, receive sim, say nothing of where it came from or why so little.

She is a trader. She works at Harvey Oak, though I found her here instead. Perhaps she has her own accounts, her own ways of moving goods.

I speak. To her, directly, or to the room in a way that calls her aside. The words matter less than the action. Debt named is half settled. But some debts you carry in silence.       They all heard. No matter. The words were soft, and Ainsley will understand what I need. She knows me, knows my silences, knows that copper in my hand means the outcrop and the work.

What do I say now? I have three units of ore. I need sim. She trades. This should be simple.

But the seam is thin, has been thin, and I cannot say that out loud in this room. Cannot let Perrin hear that the copper is running out, that the household might face scarcity, that our name could carry the taint of debt I have already incurred but not confessed.

I step closer. Lower my voice, or hope she reads my face. Trade the ore. Get sim. Move the day forward.

"I have copper. Three units. You trade at Harvey Oak. What can you give me for it?"

Not enough to pay Marta. Not enough to clear my name. But sim in hand, moving toward that 400, is better than ore in my pack and silence between me and my creditor.         I have nothing in my hands now. The copper ore is hers, passed across the space between us without a word of price, of value, of what I need in return.

She holds it. She looks at me, perhaps, or she doesn't. The room is full - Tobias, Perrin, Nell - and I have given away my morning's work with no guarantee, no number, no settlement.

This is trust, or this is foolishness. Twenty years married, and we have never said plainly that she runs the money and I bring it in. But she knows. She must know.

"For the household," I say, if I say anything. Or I say nothing, let the silence stand.

I need sim. She has the copper. She trades. If she does not offer me sim now, I must ask, or I must wait, or I must live with the weight of another uncertainty added to the debt I already carry.

What will she do? What will I do? The day moves on. The 400 sim still sits between me and Marta Thorne. And the seam is still thin, and I am still alone in that knowledge, even if Ainsley guesses.

I wait. Words spent. Action taken. Now the room answers.

I stand in my own home, copper gone from my hands, and Nell's words hit like a seam collapsing. Forty years ago she moved a marker. The Thornes have been polite about the wrong family. And my father—she knew my father's silences, his debts paid in work rather than words.

I have 2718 sim now. Ainsley must have paid me for the copper, or passed me value somehow, while I stood there with my mouth closed and my hands open. I did not see it happen. Did not name the price. Did not settle anything at the table.

Nell sees me. Sees the trap my father walked into. The same trap I am in now—debt to the Thornes, silence about money, dignity mistaken for secrecy.

"Ainsley," I say, and I do not look at Perrin or Tobias or even Nell, though her words deserve an answer. "I have 400 sim owed to Marta Thorne. The seam has been thin five weeks. I told no one. Not even you."

The words cost nothing but pride. Pride is cheaper than silence, in the end.

"I want to pay it in one piece. Named out loud. Not in installments, not in favors, not in the civil words that mean 'you still owe me.'"

I pause. The room breathes. Nell knows something about markers and Thornes and forty years of politeness covering the wrong name. I will ask her, but not now. Not until I have settled my own debt plain.

"Give me until I can face Marta with the full weight. Or tell me I am a fool for waiting. But do not let me walk into my father's silence thinking it is dignity."

I look at Nell then. The marker by the wheat strip. The debt she paid already, in another man's name.

"And you," I say. "The Thornes and the wrong family. That is your telling, not mine. But I hear it." </think>  The words are out. The debt named in my own house, in front of my wife, my children, my sister-in-law who knew my father's silences before I was born. I cannot take them back. Do not want to.

Perrin heard. The student, my child, knows now that the family is short. I swore I would not let that happen—would not let a child of mine be told we carry debt. But naming it is different than being told. Naming it is half settled. The rest is work.

I have 2718 sim. Need 400 more to reach Marta with one clean payment. Can I earn that today? Tomorrow? The seam is thin, has been thin, and three units this morning barely moved the needle.

I could borrow from Ainsley. From the household. But then I trade one silence for another, owe my wife what I owe Marta, and the weight just shifts.

I look at Nell. The marker by the wheat strip. Forty years of politeness about the wrong family.

"We'll see," I say to her, though I mean no. Not yet. Not until I understand what she knows about Thornes and markers and debts that outlast the men who made them.

Time passes. The conversation breathes. I have said what I needed to say—to Ainsley, to the room, to the weight I have carried alone for weeks. Now I need to move, work, earn, or this naming will be just another empty thing my father would have done.
